list.listitem: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a short-term neurologic disorder more common in the elderly and normally caused by embolic or occlusive atherosclerotic disease. C
TIA should be considered a "stroke-prone" state with the majority of the 90-day risk for stroke occurring in the first week after the TIA. A
Acute neuroimaging is recommended by US and European guidelines as part of the initial evaluation.C
Antihypertensive treatment, statin agents, and smoking cessation counseling and therapies are recommended to reduce recurrent stroke. A

ACC/AHA guidelines recommend antiplatelet therapy. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is recommended for up to 21 days is recommended for patients with high risk TIA, severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis, or minor stroke.A
Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is strongly recommended for patients with ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 70% to 99% and anticoagulation for patients with an identified cardioembolic source. A
Instruct patients to call 911 or seek immediate care if they suspect a TIA, even if symptoms improve after a few minutes. C

background.definition: TIA is a brief episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain or retinal ischemia, with clinical symptoms typically lasting less than an hour, and without evidence of acute infarction. The previous definition of a TIA—a cerebral dysfunction of an ischemic nature lasting no longer than 24 hours with a tendency to recur—is no longer recommended.

list.listitem: 0.68 to 0.83 new cases per 1000 persons per year.
Males and blacks have higher rates of TIA.
For men prevalence ranges from 27/1000 men between the ages of 65 and 69 years to 36/1000 men between the ages of 75 and 79 years.
For women prevalence ranges from 16/1000 women between the ages of 65 and 69 years to 41/1000 women between the ages of 75 and 79 years.
In a nationwide survey of older individuals reporting no prior history of stroke or TIA, detailed questioning found that the prevalence of one or more stroke/TIA symptoms was almost 18%.
About half of patients experiencing TIA do not report it to their healthcare clinician.
Fifteen percent to thirty percent of patients with stroke have had a prior TIA.
Large vessel atherosclerotic vascular disease
Cardiogenic emboli
Small vessel atherosclerotic vascular disease
Nonatherosclerotic vasculopathies
Hypercoagulable states
Regional reduction or cessation of blood flow to the brain results in transient focal neurologic symptoms without evidence of infarction.
The pathophysiology of TIA is similar to that of stroke, but why similar events produce a TIA in one individual and stroke in another is unknown.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Cardiac causes (eg, acute myocardial infarction [MI], atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, etc)
Ratio of apolipoproteins B to A1

list.listitem: Primary prevention is directed toward reduction of risk factors for TIA and atherosclerotic disease. A
Screening for TIA is not recommended.
The USPSTF concluded that evidence was insufficient regarding screening persons without a history of TIA or stroke for atrial fibrillation.
See chapter on stroke for screening recommendations regarding that condition.
Primary prevention is directed toward reduction of risk factors for TIA and atherosclerotic disease.
The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis (CAS) in the general adult population.

For subjects with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with an annual estimated stroke risk of less than 4%, aspirin reduces the first occurrence of stroke or TIA (NNT = 100). In higher risk patients, anticoagulation with warfarin further reduces the risk of first stroke or TIA when compared to aspirin therapy.

In subjects with diabetes mellitus, daily low dose aspirin reduces the risk of TIA (NNT = 90). Low dose aspirin in patients with diabetes have an increased risk of major bleeding episodes, but with no effects on vascular or all-cause deaths.
See chapter on stroke for secondary prevention recommendations regarding TIA and stroke.
The definition of TIA has recently been updated to include a duration of symptoms typically less than an hour without evidence of infarction. C
Acute onset of facial paresis, arm drift, and abnormal speech are the most predictive symptoms and signs of TIA or stroke. C
Acute neuroimaging is required for all patients presenting with TIA to exclude mimics of TIA, to assess for infarction, and to assist in treatment planning and suitability for intervention.C
MRA has better test characteristics than duplex ultrasound in the detection of severe stenosis (70%-99% occlusion). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Often accompanied by scotoma, headache, or nausea prior to onset of neurologic deficits, which may be gradual in onset
Often accompanied by uncontrollable movements and altered consciousness prior to neurologic deficits, which persist after the event. Rapid onset can mimic TIA
Re-expression of prior cerebral infarction may occur during infection
Associated with loss of consciousness but no focal deficits afterward
Abnormality on head CT or MRI

list.listitem: Factors associated with increased likelihood of TIA include: focal neurologic deficit persisting less than 24 hours (most <1 h) in the absence of a history of head trauma or radiologic evidence of infarction.

The modified Explicit Diagnostic Criteria for TIA have excellent accuracy (sensitivity 98.4%, specificity 73.8%, LR+ 3.8, LR- 0.02):
A: Sudden onset of a fully reversible visual or neurological symptoms B: Duration <24 hours C: At least 2 of the following All symptoms are maximal in less than 1 minute with no gradual spread All symptoms occur simultaneously All symptoms are deficits (e.g. no irritative symptoms such as photopsias, pins and needles) No headache accompanies or follows the neurological symptoms within one hour
D: None of the following isolated symptoms (they may occur together with more typical symptoms): shaking spells, diplopia, dizziness, vertigo, syncope, decreased level of consciousness, confusion, hyperventilation associated paresthesia, unexplained falls, and amnesia. E: No evidence of acute infarction in the relevant area on neuroimaging.
Acute onset of facial paresis, arm drift, and abnormal speech are the most predictive symptoms and signs of TIA or stroke.
Auscultation of a bruit is only modestly helpful at ruling in or ruling out high-grade stenosis.
Acute neuroimaging (MRA or CTA) is recommended for all patients presenting with TIA to exclude mimics of TIA and to assess for infarction. This is recommended by US and European guidelines.

US joint guidelines recommend non-contrast CT +/- CTA for TIA patients with evidence of intracranial hemorrhage. If not and endovascular therapy is considered then NCCT plus digital subtraction angiography is recommended, or NCCT with CT angiography with or without perfusion CT, or MR imaging + MR angiography. The guideline has more detailed information including a diagnostic algorithm that should be consulted.
Assess for the presence of atrial fibrillation by history, ECG, and cardiac monitoring.
Assess patients with TIA for carotid stenosis using noninvasive testing.
Contrast-enhanced MRA, CT angiography, and ultrasound are nearly comparable as the preferred imaging studies for detecting high-grade carotid stenosis.
Consider a transthoracic echocardiogram to evaluate for structural heart disease that could lead to embolism (i.e., cardiomyopathy, atrial septal defect).
The Canadian TIA Risk Score has been prospectively validated in 7607 consecutive patients presenting to the ED with TIA or minor stroke.
The Cincinnati Stroke Scale can identify patients in community and primary care settings who are likely to have stroke ().
The Los Angeles Prehospital Stroke Screen is a similar rule that has also been prospectively validated ().
The Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room (ROSIER) scale is a similar rule that has also been prospectively validated in emergency departments.
The ABCD rule is a validated rule to predict stroke within 7 and 30 days after TIA, although recent studies have drawn into question the clinical efficacy of this tool.
See .

In patients in whom typical atherosclerotic risk factors are not present, for example, the young, screen for a hypercoagulable state and consider transesophogeal echocardiogram to look for atrial septal abnormalities and emboli.

Two scales have been evaluated to aid first responders in the diagnosis of stroke. In principle, these scales, the Cinncinati Prehospital Stroke Scale (see ) and Los Angeles Prehospital Stroke Screens (see ), can be applied to the diagnosis of TIA.
Perform CBC, UA, Chem 7, PT/PTT, and ECG in all patients.

For detection of carotid stenosis, a recent meta-analysis found that noninvasive testing (including duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, MRA, and contrast-enhanced MRI) all had high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing 70% to 99% stenosis. AHA guidelines (2023) recommend CT angiography as the preferred study. If it can be performed promptly MR angiography is an acceptable and accurate alternative for imaging the carotids.
In patients presenting with TIA and normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG, no studies have evaluated the optimal duration of monitoring to detect occult or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

Perform transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in all patients presenting with TIA to detect other cardioembolic sources. Possible etiologies detected by echocardiography include valvular vegetation, myxoma, or left ventricular thrombus (in the setting of dilated cardiomyopathy). Large atheroma in the proximal aorta and aortic arch can also be causes of cerebral emboli. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) can be considered in patients with high suspicion for cardioembolic source but a negative TTE.

Perform acute neuroimaging for all patients presenting with TIA to exclude mimics of TIA and to assess for infarction. For both indications, MRI and its modalities are superior to CT. CT is adequate to make decisions in the emergency setting if MRI is not available.

AHA guidelines recognize that non-contrast CT is a pragmatic initial choice for imaging, but recommend multimodal MRI as the preferred study. Patients with diffusion weighted imaging lesions on MRI are 6 times more likely to have a recurrent stroke at one year.
Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is strongly recommended in persons with symptomatic carotid stenosis over 70%. A
Anticoagulation is strongly recommended in persons with atrial fibrillation; for persons without atrial fibrillation, antiplatelet therapy is recommended. A
DAPT for up to 21 days is recommended for patients with high risk TIA, severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis, or minor stroke.A

Control of atherosclerotic risk factors such as reduction of blood pressure, A reduction of low-density lipoprotein, A and cessation of smoking B lowers the risk of subsequent atherosclerotic disease.
Expedited evaluation and initiation of secondary prevention therapy has been shown to reduce the rate of stroke following TIA. B

For persons with noncardioembolic TIA or minor stroke, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel, ticagrelor, or prasugrel) is recommended based on a meta-analysis of 17 studies with 27,358 patients. Initiating DAPT (most studies used clopidogrel 75 mg once daily) within 24 hours after onset of symptoms of minor stroke or TIA reduces the risk of recurrent stroke (NNT = 50) with the greatest net benefit in the first 10 days. The systematic review concluded that for every 1000 persons with minor stroke or TIA treated with aspirin + clopidogrel instead of monotherapy, there would be 20 fewer strokes and 2 more major hemorrhages. The meta-analysis also found that treatment beyond 30 days did not reduce the risk of stroke any further, but was associated with more hemorrhages. A second less comprehensive meta-analysis of DAPT versus monothearpy had similar findings.

ACC/AHA guidelines recommend antiplatelet monotherapy following TIA. They recommend DAPT for up to 21 days only for patients with high risk TIA, severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis, or minor stroke.

The THALES trial enrolled 11,016 patients with high risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke and found that compared with aspirin alone, aspirin + ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily reduced the likelhood of stroke at 30 days (NNT = 68, 95% CI 42 to 175) but also increased the risk of major bleeding (NNTH 922).

A network meta-analysis identified 9 studies with 22,098 participants comparing ticagrelor vs clopidogrel in addition to aspirin in patients with TIA or minor ischemic stroke. Dual therapy with both was associated with less disability and death at 90 days compared with aspirin alone with most of the benefit coming from ischemic stroke prevention rather than mortality. Clopidogrel had a more favorable safety profile than ticagrelor.

A secondary analysis of a randomized trial comparing aspirin with aspirin plus clopidogrel after TIA or minor stroke found a low risk of major hemorrhage: 0.9% in those on dual therapy and 0.2% in those on aspirin alone over a 3 month period.

In a multicenter trial from China, investigators included patients with ischemic stroke with an NIHSS score of < 5 or high-risk TIAs who presented up to 72 hours of symptom onset. The 6100 patients were randomized to receive clopidogrel plus aspirin or matching placebo plus aspirin.vFor the primary efficacy outcome of a new ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke within 90 days, the clopidogrel-aspirin group fared better (7.3% vs 9.2%, p = 0.008, NNT = 53). They were also more likely to experience moderate-to-severe bleeding (0.9% vs 0.4%, P = .03, NNTH = 200).

A Chinese RCT of 6412 patients who were carriers of CYP2C19 loss of function alleles found that when used with aspirin as DAPT following minor ischemic stroke or TIA, ticagrelor was associated with fewer subsequent strokes (6.0% vs 7.3%, NNT = 77) but more bleeding events (5.3% vs 2.5%, NNTH = 36).
CV risk factor management
Antihypertensive treatment and statin agents are recommended by AHA/ACC guidelines (2021) to reduce recurrent stroke.
Smoking cessation is also recommend, along with exercise.

Lower LDL targets after ischemic stroke achieved via statin therapy reduce major cardiovascular events (NNT = 43 over 3.5 years), but with the greatest benefit seen in those presenting with an index event of acute stroke (rather than TIA).

Anticoagulation with adjusted-dose warfarin (range 2.0-3.0) is strongly recommended for persons with atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter. New oral anticoagulants such as direct thrombin inhibitors or factor Xa inhibitors may be reasonable alternatives to warfarin. Anticoagulation is not recommended for patients with TIA but no evidence of atrial fibrillation of a cardioembolic source of TIA/stroke. Anticoagulation bears a higher risk than antiplatelet therapy for extracranial bleeding.

CEA is strongly recommended for persons with ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 70% to 99%; CEA can be considered for persons with ipsilateral carotid stenosis of 50% to 69%. There is less clear benefit in patients with near-total occlusion or for stenosis less than 50%. These recommendations apply to patients who are eligible candidates for surgery and who are able to receive care from surgeons with low complication rates (<7% risk of stroke or death).

While initial studies suggested that carotid stenting is inferior to carotid endarterectomy for 6-month risk of stroke or death (NNH = 18), a more recent trial demonstrated that for the longer term carotid artery stenting is equivalent to carotid endarterectomy for the outcomes of stroke, myocardial infarction or death. In the periprocedural period, CAS is associated with a higher stroke risk while CEA is associated with a higher risk of MI.
A clinical rule has been developed and validated to determine prognosis in patients undergoing CEA.
Percutaneous closure of a patent foramen ovale has not been shown to provide advantage over medical therapy with aspirin or warfarin for patients with TIA at the end of 2 years of follow-up.

The rationale for hospitalization is predicated on the premise that earlier diagnosis of a remediable condition (e.g., ipsilateral carotid disease or a cardioembolic source) will lead to improved outcomes. While no RCT data confirm this hypothesis, two observational studies found substantially improved outcomes associated with expedited evaluation and initiation of secondary prevention therapy after TIA.

The decision to hospitalize could be based on time since TIA, a clinical prediction rule (ABCD2 score), or other patient factors such as transport, presence of comorbid disease, and reliability of follow-up.
Optimal inpatient care would include monitoring for cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and atrial fibrillation.
Also perform rapid head and carotid imaging.
Give antihypertensive, antiplatelet, and lipid-lowering therapy.
Thirty minutes of moderate-intensity physical exercise most days for those capable of physical activity is recommended to reduce risk factors and comorbid conditions.
Consider TIA a "stroke-prone" state with risks of CVA after TIA of 3.9% at 48 hours and 5.5% at a week. A
TIA patients are also at increased risk for MI and death from nonstroke vascular causes. B
The ABCD2 score has limited value in predicting the risk of stroke after TIA. B
Instruct patients to call 911 or seek immediate care if they suspect a TIA, even if symptoms improve after a few minutes. C
Consider TIA a "stroke-prone" state.

The absolute risks of CVA after TIA in observational studies have been 3.9% (1.4%-4.9%) at 48 hours, 5.5% (3%-8.6%) at a week, and 10% to 20% at 90 days. Fully 60% of the 90-day CVA risk after TIA is over the week following the TIA.
Fifteen percent to twenty-six percent of patients with CVA have had preceding TIAs, about 40% of which occurred within the prior 7 days.
The risks for nonstroke vascular death and MI are each about 2% per year following TIA, with the time immediately following a TIA posing the greatest risk.

Currently no RCTs have studied whether more rapid diagnosis and therapy improve outcomes after TIA. Two observational studies have found improved outcomes associated with expedited evaluation and initiation of secondary prevention therapy after TIA.
One clinical prediction rule for TIA is the ABCD2 score, shown in . The likelihood ratios for this rule are modestly helpful.
Other factors associated with increased risk of stroke after TIA include a prior stroke, new infarction on initial head CT, and diffusion-weighted imaging lesions on MRI.

The optimal strategy to reduce risk of nonstroke vascular death and MI following TIA has not been established. Options include maximizing coronary heart disease (CHD) risk reduction therapy in all patients after TIA or targeting CHD therapy guided by either universal or symptom-driven noninvasive CHD testing.

Signs of TIA or stroke of which patients should be aware include: (1) sudden confusion or trouble speaking; (2) numbness or weakness of face, arm, or leg; (3) sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes; (4) sudden trouble walking, dizziness, or loss of balance; and (5) severe headache with no known cause.
Instruct patients to call 911 or seek immediate care if they suspect a TIA, even if symptoms improve after a few minutes.

cell.label: Patient with suspected new TIA (no fixed deficit at time of presentation)
Speech deficit, unilateral motor loss, or unilateral sensory loss?
Reassess whether patient has TIA; consider neurologic consultation.
Dexstick, CBC, Chem 7, PT/PTT, UA, ECG/cardiac monitoring, noncontrast head CT.
Glucose or electrolyte abnormalities, atrial fibrillation, intracranial mass, bleed?
Perform expedited workup for stroke As an inpatient or in the ER.
Did event occur within 7 days and ABCD2 5 or more?
Schedule workup that should be completed within 1 wk.

footnotes.footnote: Expedited workup consists of noninvasive carotid imaging (contrast-enhanced neck MRA, neck MRA, carotid duplex ultrasonography, or CTA), and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Perform transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) in patients <45 y old and in patients whose presentation is suspicious for emboli.

feature.caption: Los Angeles Prehospital Stroke Screen.
feature.feature_body: Presence of all of the following six items strongly suggests stroke (91% sensitive, 97% specific, LR+ 31, LR− 0.09): Age >45 y No seizure history Symptoms present <24 h Ambulatory at baseline Serum glucose between 60 and 400 mg/dL Unilateral deficit of one of three items (facial paresis, arm drift, weak grip) From Kidwell CS, Starkman S, Eckstein M, Weems K, Saver JL. Identifying stroke in the field. Prospective validation of the Los Angeles prehospital stroke screen (LAPSS). Stroke 2000;31:71–76.
